title: The Woman Who Killed Marat, and Why the Court Wouldn't Believe She Acted Alone
dek: Corday had written her declaration before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her about the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that someone from the provinces would think Marat a monster.
why: High information density, weaving the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain; the second half's assassination details are especially valuable.
who: Listeners interested in the French Revolution, the origins of the Terror, and the mechanics of political violence; readers who want to understand how populist language and revolutionary institutions get improvised.
skip: The last two minutes are a trailer for another podcast, with no historical content, and can be skipped.

points.h: The assassination declaration was written before the act
points.body: When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile scoundrel," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and therefore is outside the law," and called on the French to "rise up. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc justification; it was written before the act — what she wanted was not escape, but to turn her death into a rallying point.

points.h: Marat was the first modern populist
points.body: Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His formula included: constantly invoking the capitalized "People," claiming the people are at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theories, openly stating his goal was to keep readers "perpetually alert," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and the like. The episode points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

points.h: Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
points.body: In early 1793 France suffered successive poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government, lacking money for war, could only print paper money, the assignat, with about four billion in circulation. This caused severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, protests occurred almost daily in the markets, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The episode stresses: these were the same conditions that had originally sparked the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "The Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

points.h: The commander's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
points.body: On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counter-attacked, defeating Dumouriez at Neerwinden, forcing him to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, asking his subordinates, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking with him a number of senior officers, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. A volunteer wrote to his mother: "Whom can we trust now?"

The episode stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint, no plan; they were built as they went along, only later appearing as a machine, and many who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal, located in the Palais de Justice in Paris, with the existing Conciergerie prison in its basement. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

points.h: The Girondins used new rules to strike back at Marat, and it backfired
points.body: Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins, taking advantage of the many deputies away in the provinces, indicted Marat on 14 April, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat hid for three days, then, finding that Parisian street opinion was on his side, turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the trial opened at the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and allowed Marat a long self-defence. The ten-man jury acquitted him within hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by about 800 people, wearing a crown of roses, chanting "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

points.h: Corday buys a knife: a 15 cm black-handled kitchen knife
points.body: Around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the Palais-Royal arcades, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing her white Norman-style hat. She entered a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 cm long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but without an appointment she was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

points.h: The court wouldn't believe a woman could act alone
points.body: Corday was arrested on the spot; one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognised Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the one who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that people from the provinces would think Marat a bad man.
